headline: A 66-year-old nurse is facing down retirement with just $500 saved. Who's to blame?

paragraphs.text: 'Retirement is a financial status, not an age'
"When you spend every dollar on lifestyle habits and car loans for decades instead of saving, you don't get to act surprised when the math doesn't work." (Photo subject is a model.)

Regarding the 66-year-old nurse (I'm 66, rely on Social Security and have just $500 in savings. What hope do I have?) having less than $500 to her name after a career in nursing isn't bad luck - it's the result of lifelong financial choices. Even putting aside $1,000-a-year over a few decades would have left her in a completely different position.

It's her fault. Retiring with zero savings isn't a viable plan, and there's no point in worrying about Social Security earnings limits when you don't have enough to live on. She didn't have a low-wage job; she had a solid career as a nurse, which makes the lack of a basic budget or safety net all the more frustrating.

When you spend every dollar on lifestyle habits and car loans for decades instead of saving, you don't get to act surprised when the math doesn't work. Retirement is a financial status, not an age - and without savings, she simply can't afford to stop working until 70. This is the problem with America. No one wants to be held accountable, even to themselves.
How many Starbucks did she have a week?

She could have been living paycheck-to-paycheck like millions of Americans or she could have, as you say in your letter, lost sight of the bigger picture.
Asking "why?" is often a fruitful question, if we keep an open mind.

We don't know how much that nurse was paid, and we don't know whether she was divorced or had difficulty paying rent. She could have lived paycheck-to-paycheck on stagnant wages and lost sight of the challenges that lie ahead. Most nurses work grueling 12-hour shifts. They don't retire out of entitlement; they retire because their knees and backs have given out.

Kindness is free, and it's often key to understanding what went right and wrong in people's lives, including our own. The average annual salary for nurses rose over the past 30 years from roughly $40,000 in the 2000s to $97,500 today, but those salaries depend on the medical facility, city/town and specialty. That income falls to $42,000 a year for nursing assistants and $64,400 for licensed vocational nurses.

I don't wish to change your view of her circumstances or why she is in the position she is in. Your views are your own. Yes, we all must take responsibility for our situation in life. We agree on that. But I prefer to frame her story as one of roads not taken and financial literacy, or lack thereof. She may also have had a catastrophic life event: divorce, a medical crisis or caring for an elderly relative.
Kindness is free and it's often key to understanding what went wrong.

This woman, for better or for worse, felt left out of the political discourse and conversations centering members of the middle class as a person who is living close to the poverty line. She collects $2,000 in Social Security, and also suggested that she is scared about what will happen when she is no longer able to work. She lives in a two-bedroom apartment with a roommate who is receiving disability benefits.

She may not be aware: When she reaches her full retirement age - 66 and 10 months or 67 years of age - there is no limit on how much she can earn without reducing how much she receives in Social Security benefits. Best of all, if any benefits were withheld earlier, the Social Security Administration will recalculate and increase her monthly check once she hits her FRA.

The nurse whose situation frustrates you is not unique. Multiple studies contend that just under half of retirees have less than $100,000 saved for retirement and, according to a 2025 report from the Transamerica Institute, 12% of retirees have no savings, and more than half (53%) rely on Social Security as their primary source of income throughout their retirement.

Financial fragility

"Retirees face financial fragility, especially being vulnerable to economic uncertainty, inflation, rising healthcare costs, and financial market volatility - all factors that can easily erode their buying power on limited income," the report said. "Many are concerned about their health in older age and their ability to afford long-term care, yet many also have not solidified plans."

Achieving a secure retirement is, for some people, easier on paper. Lower-income workers who come up short in retirement often did not have a 401(k) at work, for instance, and research suggests that they tend to be women, who still experience a gender pay gap in part due to the kinds of jobs they have traditionally inhabited, as well as single adults and racial minorities.

Financial literacy has improved in recent decades. One study by researchers from Texas Tech University and the University of Michigan found that financial literacy declines steadily in older age, even though confidence in money-related decisions remains high. Average financial literacy scores increase up to 50 years of age and then begin to fall with age, they concluded.
Not everyone has the same start in life and chooses well-paid careers.

Access to education plays a role. Some 81% of college graduates versus 39% of adults with no college education have savings, and 68% of non-Hispanic white adults have a retirement savings plan versus 42% of people of color, Gallup found. Men (61%) are also more likely than women (57%) to have a retirement plan. (Women are more likely to be caretakers and homemakers.)

There's a lot, in fairness, that goes into making up the puzzle of any person's life story. Did I have an inheritance? What career did I choose? Was there a 401(k)? Did I suffer from an unexpected job loss, or a downturn in the market just as I was entering retirement? If we are honest, our journeys are a combination of upbringing, hard work, planning and dumb luck.

The 66-year-old's Social Security suggests she probably worked as hard as you or me. You learned either from your peers, parents or reading the financial press and, regardless of your profession, did not live above your means because you knew you had to put money aside for retirement and because you had the ability to do so. That's smart and savvy. But not everyone has the same start in life or chooses a well-paid career.
Some people have a margin of error to learn from their mistakes; others, alas, don't.
